title: Tangel v. Commissioner
subject: Substantial Rights / Funded Research
summary: Tangel v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2021-1) is a U.S. Tax Court ruling on the R&D tax credit funded research exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H). It applies to contract manufacturers and engineering firms: when customer purchase orders give the client exclusive rights to research results, the contractor retains no substantial rights and loses 100% of Section 41 credits on that project.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background

On January 11, 2021, the United States Tax Court issued its memorandum opinion in Tangel v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-1 (Docket Nos. 27268-13, 27309-13, 27371-13, 27373-13, 27374-13, and 27375-13), authored by Judge Albert G. Lauber. The ruling stands as a watershed decision in federal research and development (R&D) tax credit jurisprudence under Section 41 of the Internal Revenue Code (IRC), establishing a strict, contract-centric standard for evaluating the "funded research" exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d). For custom manufacturers, engineering firms, systems integrators, and contract developers operating in the United States, the decision demonstrates that regardless of the technical complexity or engineering novelty of a project, standard intellectual property ownership and use-restriction clauses in customer purchase orders can completely disqualify a taxpayer from claiming Section 41 research credits on a project as a matter of law.
Factual Context and the Taxpayer's Claim

The petitioners in the consolidated litigation—Edward J. and Beatrice C. Tangel, Jeffrey and Kathleen Tangel, Lawrence E. and Karen S. Tangel, Douglas J. and Juanita V. Tangel, Neil R. and Gyneen W. Tangel, and Gerald Landry and Colette Tangel—were the shareholders of Enercon Engineering, Inc. ("Enercon"), an S corporation domiciled in the United States. Enercon operated as a specialized designer and producer of integrated controls and switchgears for custom applications in the power generation industry.

For the 2008, 2009, and 2010 tax years, Enercon claimed federal credits for increasing research activities under IRC § 41 totaling $929,668 across 142 separate engineering and manufacturing projects. Because Enercon was organized as an S corporation, the claimed Section 41 credits flowed through directly to the individual petitioners on their personal federal income tax returns.

The specific dispute adjudicated in T.C. Memo. 2021-1 centered on Project No. 37688, a major custom engineering engagement undertaken by Enercon for Vericor Power Systems, LLC ("Vericor") beginning in February 2009. Under this engagement, Vericor hired Enercon to develop, according to existing designs, a new enclosure for turbine power generation, requiring Enercon to provide assembly, system integration, controls engineering, and packaging for one new power generation unit, alongside the redesign and retrofitting of three existing turbine units. The commercial arrangement was executed through an initial General Purchase Order valued at $951,954 and subsequently expanded through 18 sequential change orders, culminating in 19 total purchase orders with an aggregate contract value of $1,423,847.
The Tax Authority's Challenge and Procedural Posture

Following an examination of Enercon's 2008–2010 tax returns, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) disallowed the claimed $929,668 in pass-through research credits and issued notices of deficiency to the shareholder petitioners. The petitioners timely petitioned the U.S. Tax Court to redetermine the deficiencies. Because litigating 142 distinct engineering projects individually would have been protracted and burdensome, in early 2018—while the IRS's motion for partial summary judgment was pending—the parties selected a representative sample of projects to be tried, with the Tax Court addressing the sampling methodology in an order dated February 22, 2018, after the parties were unable to agree on a method. In establishing the trial sample, the parties carved out two major engagements from the sampling frame: Project No. 34788, which was to be evaluated separately because of its large size, and Project No. 37688 (the Vericor project), which was to be evaluated separately because of the IRS's motion for partial summary judgment under Tax Court Rule 121, filed on September 12, 2017.

In its motion for partial summary judgment, the IRS asserted two primary grounds for disallowance regarding the Vericor project: first, that the research activities conducted by Enercon under Project No. 37688 were 100% "funded" by Vericor within the meaning of IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) because Enercon failed to retain "substantial rights" in the research results under Vericor's governing contract terms; and second, that the petitioners had not substantiated the amount of qualified research expenses (QREs) incurred on this project.
Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

In the United States, tax credits are strictly a matter of legislative grace, and the taxpayer bears the affirmative burden of proving absolute entitlement to the claimed credit under Tax Court Rule 142(a) and established Supreme Court precedent such as INDOPCO, Inc. v. Commissioner, 503 U.S. 79 (1992). Congress originally enacted the research credit in 1981—following the earlier 1954 enactment of IRC § 174 for research and experimental deductions—and subsequently modified and redesignated it as IRC § 41 in the Tax Reform Act of 1986 before making it permanent in the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act of 2015. IRC § 41(a) and (c) allow taxpayers a credit equal to 20 percent of the amount by which their QREs for the taxable year exceed a statutory base amount. Under IRC § 41(b)(1)–(3), QREs are bifurcated into two categories: "in-house research expenses"—comprising wages paid or incurred to an employee for qualified services (engaging in, directly supervising, or directly supporting qualified research) and amounts paid or incurred for supplies used in the conduct of qualified research—and "contract research expenses," which allow a taxpayer to claim 65 percent of amounts paid or incurred to a third party performing qualified research on the taxpayer's behalf.

To qualify as "qualified research" under IRC § 41(d)(1), activities must satisfy a stringent Four-Part Test—requiring that expenses qualify under Section 174, seek to discover information that is technological in nature, be intended for the development of a new or improved business component, and substantially all constitute elements of a process of experimentation—and must not fall within eight enumerated statutory exclusions set forth in IRC § 41(d)(4), such as research after commercial production, adaptation of existing business components, duplication, or foreign research. Chief among these exclusions in commercial contracting is IRC § 41(d)(4)(H), which mandates that qualified research shall not include "any research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person (or governmental entity)".

Whereas IRC § 174 historically permitted both a paying client and a performing contractor to deduct their respective research expenditures, Congress determined when enacting the Section 41 tax credit that the subsidy should be allocated to only one party rather than duplicated across both. Because the statute itself does not define the term "funded," Treasury promulgated regulations designed to prevent both the contracting customer and the performing contractor from claiming the Section 41 credit on the same underlying research activities—an architecture commonly referred to in tax jurisprudence as the "mirror rules." Pursuant to Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(9), determining the extent to which research is funded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) is governed directly by Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d).

Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) establishes a two-pronged inquiry to evaluate whether research performed under a third-party contract is funded. Under the first prong—the Financial Risk Test (Contingency of Payment) set forth in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1)—amounts payable under any agreement that are contingent on the success of the research are considered paid for the product or result of the research rather than for the performance of the research itself, and therefore are not treated as "funding." In such arrangements, the performing contractor bears the financial risk of technical failure and may claim the research credit, whereas the paying customer is barred from claiming contract research expenses under the mirror rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2).

Under the second prong—the Substantial Rights Test set forth in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2) and (d)(3)—regardless of the financial risk posture, a performing taxpayer is entitled to the research credit only if it retains "substantial rights" in the research. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2), if a taxpayer performing research for another person retains no substantial rights in the research under the agreement providing for the research, the research is treated as fully funded for purposes of IRC § 41(d)(4)(H), and zero expenses paid or incurred by the contractor constitute QREs. Specifically, a taxpayer retains no substantial rights if the contract "confers on another person the exclusive right to exploit the results of the research" or if the taxpayer "must pay for the right to use the results of the research" under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i). Furthermore, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2) explicitly dictates that "incidental benefits to the taxpayer from performance of the research (for example, increased experience in a field of research) do not constitute substantial rights in the research".

If—and only if—a taxpayer retains substantial rights in the research while receiving non-contingent payments, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i) treats the research as funded "to the extent of the payments (and fair market value of any property) to which the taxpayer becomes entitled by performing the research", permitting a partial credit allocation on a project-by-project basis only where total project research expenses exceed the funding received. Under this allocation rule, funding stacks first against otherwise creditable expenses unless the taxpayer establishes to the satisfaction of the IRS that total research expenses exceed funding and otherwise creditable expenses exceed 65 percent of the payment, in which case funding may be allocated proportionately.
The Court's Final Holding and Jurisprudential Outlook

The U.S. Tax Court granted the IRS's motion for partial summary judgment in full regarding Project No. 37688. Applying the Federal Circuit's precedent in Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000), Judge Lauber held that whether a taxpayer retains substantial rights must be determined strictly by examining the terms of the research agreements executed by the contracting parties. Analyzing Paragraph 15 ("Designs, Drawings and Data") of Vericor's standard Terms and Conditions alongside Enercon's own summary offer letter, the Court concluded that the contract conferred upon Vericor the exclusive right to exploit the results of the research and stripped Enercon of any right to reuse the technical information, designs, or tooling developed for the project without Vericor's prior written consent.

Because Enercon retained no substantial rights in the research performed under the Vericor purchase orders, the research was deemed 100% funded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2), resulting in the complete disallowance of all QREs associated with Project No. 37688. Crucially, because the contractual disqualification was absolute as a matter of law, the Tax Court expressly declined to evaluate the IRS's alternative argument that petitioners had not substantiated the amount of qualified research expenses incurred on Project No. 37688. Subsequent federal appellate and Tax Court decisions—including Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024) and Smith v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-50 (2026), which rejected a challenge to the validity of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) under Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo—have cemented Tangel as foundational authority governing the substantial rights inquiry across the United States.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

The complete disqualification of Enercon's claimed R&D tax credits on the Vericor engagement stemmed from a series of compounding contractual, legal, and procedural failures. Rather than losing on the underlying engineering merits of its turbine enclosure development, the taxpayer was defeated at the summary judgment stage by the plain language of the commercial procurement documents it executed.
Failure to Assert or Establish Financial Risk Under the First Prong

In analyzing funded research under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), a threshold defense for contractors is demonstrating that customer payments were contingent on the technical success of the research under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1). However, in Tangel, the petitioners did not even contend that Vericor's payments across the 19 purchase orders ($1,423,847) were contingent upon the success of Enercon's research, forcing the Tax Court to note that the first regulatory factor was wholly inapplicable.

Even worse for the taxpayer, the structure of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) creates a fatal structural asymmetry between financial risk and intellectual property rights. While failing the Financial Risk Test (i.e., receiving guaranteed or progress-based funding) reduces creditable expenses dollar-for-dollar to the extent of customer payments under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i), failing the Substantial Rights Test under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2) triggers a 100% forfeiture of all project QREs, even if the contractor suffered a massive financial overrun where its internal research costs exceeded customer payments. By executing a contract that divested all substantial rights while failing to establish payment contingency, Enercon foreclosed both full and partial credit recovery under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3).
The Contractual Fatalities of Paragraph 15 ("Designs, Drawings and Data")

The core evidentiary failure in Tangel lay within Paragraph 15 of Vericor's standard "Terms and Conditions," incorporated into all 19 purchase orders, which systematically dismantled Enercon's claim to substantial rights through three interlocking sub-clauses and a corroborating offer letter.
Sweeping Definition of Restricted "Information" and Non-Use Covenant (Paragraph 15(A))

Paragraph 15(A) defined protected "Information" broadly to encompass three distinct categories: first, technical information supplied to Enercon by or on behalf of Vericor; second, technical information designed by Enercon at Vericor's expense; and third, technical information designed by Enercon specifically to meet Vericor-furnished technical requirements. Having swept virtually every conceivable engineering output of the turbine enclosure project into the definition of "Information," Paragraph 15(A) stipulated that in consideration of Vericor furnishing such Information and design funding, Enercon agreed not to use, or assist others in using, such Information, design funding, or tooling to develop or sell "Articles" (defined broadly as the goods and services procured under the purchase orders) or similar interchangeable or substitute articles to any third party other than Vericor without Vericor's prior written consent. The clause explicitly mandated that Enercon "shall not use or disclose such Information except in the performance of Orders for Buyer" and required the return of all Information and copies upon Vericor's request. Finally, Paragraph 15(A) contained a punitive evidentiary burden-shifting mechanism: if Enercon ever developed or sold similar articles to third parties in the future, the contract placed the affirmative legal burden on Enercon to prove that Vericor's Information, funding, or tooling was not used.
"Works Made for Hire" and Irrevocable IP Assignment (Paragraph 15(B) and 15(C))

To ensure complete alienation of intellectual property, Paragraph 15(B) dictated that all "Information prepared by Seller specifically in connection with performance of this Order, including original works of authorship created by Seller, are considered 'works made for hire' within the meaning of the U.S. Copyright Laws," designating Vericor as the statutory author and sole owner from inception. Recognizing that certain engineering designs or functional schematics might fall outside statutory "work made for hire" categories under U.S. copyright law, Paragraph 15(B) included a catch-all savings clause providing that if any work was judicially determined not to constitute a work made for hire, the purchase order automatically operated as an irrevocable assignment to Vericor of all right, title, and interest in and to such work. Additionally, Paragraph 15(C) required that, where such information was furnished to Enercon's suppliers for use in performing Vericor's orders, Enercon insert the substance of Paragraph 15 in all such orders to its subcontractors.
Damning Extrinsic Admission in Enercon's Summary Offer Letter

Compounding the restrictive language of Vericor's Terms and Conditions was an explicit written admission made by Enercon itself. In its summary offer letter submitted to Vericor at the outset of the engagement, Enercon explicitly acknowledged the total transfer of ownership, writing: "All information, equipment, etc generated as a result of this order are owned by Vericor only -- 'works for hire'". This contemporaneous document eliminated any plausibility that Paragraph 15 was an overlooked boilerplate provision or that the parties intended a shared intellectual property regime.
Judicial Rejection of the Taxpayer's Four Legal Defenses

In opposing summary judgment, the petitioners advanced four legal arguments—that Paragraph 15(A) was a standard non-disclosure agreement, that Paragraph 15(B) pertained only to patents or copyrights that no party was claiming, that Enercon retained the institutional knowledge gleaned from the research, and that Lockheed Martin supported their position—attempting to reconcile Paragraph 15 with the retention of substantial rights, each of which Judge Lauber methodically rejected.
The "Standard Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA)" Fallacy

Petitioners first argued that Paragraph 15(A) was merely a conventional confidentiality or non-disclosure provision intended solely to prevent Enercon from disseminating the technical information and specifications that Vericor supplied to enable Enercon to execute the contract. The Tax Court rejected this interpretation as incompatible with the plain text and totality of the contract. While the first prong of Paragraph 15(A) covered technical information supplied by Vericor, the second and third prongs explicitly restricted technical information designed by Enercon at Vericor's expense or to meet Vericor's technical specifications, alongside any project tooling. Judge Lauber concluded that this interpretation ignores much of the relevant contract text and that Paragraph 15(A) clearly covers the results of any research Enercon performs in the course of fulfilling the contract, rather than functioning as a mere confidentiality agreement.
The "Prior Written Consent" Illusion

In rejecting petitioners' institutional-knowledge argument, the Court also held that it does not help petitioners that Paragraph 15(A) permitted Enercon to re-use the results of its research if it first obtained Vericor's "prior written consent". The Tax Court held that a conditional ability to use research results subject to the customer's unilateral, unfettered veto destroys substantial rights. Because the contract placed zero objective conditions, good-faith requirements, or limitations on Vericor's ability to arbitrarily withhold consent, the requirement of prior written consent prevented Enercon from possessing substantial rights, as the Court explained by reference to Dynetics, Inc. & Subs. v. United States, 121 Fed. Cl. 492, 521 (2015).
The "Institutional Knowledge and Experience" Defense

Petitioners also asserted that despite the transfer of formal drawings and data, Enercon retained the "institutional knowledge," technical know-how, and engineering experience gained by its staff while solving Vericor's turbine enclosure challenges, which Enercon could deploy on future commercial projects. Judge Lauber pointed directly to the unambiguous mandate of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2), which states that "[i]ncidental benefits to the taxpayer from performance of the research (for example, increased experience in a field of research) do not constitute substantial rights in the research". Retaining a more skilled or experienced workforce is an inevitable byproduct of performing any technical service; if such generalized know-how satisfied the substantial rights test, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2) would be rendered superfluous.
Misapplication of Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States

Finally, petitioners relied heavily on Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000), rev'g 42 Fed. Cl. 485 (1998), arguing that practical or regulatory limitations on selling identical articles to third parties do not negate substantial rights. The Tax Court exposed a fundamental distinction between the two cases. In Lockheed Martin, the government conceded that the defense contracts themselves granted Lockheed the legal right to use the research results in its commercial business; the Court of Federal Claims had denied the credit only because external federal export control laws referenced in the contracts restricted Lockheed's functional ability to use the research results. The Federal Circuit reversed, holding that external statutory restrictions unrelated to the research agreement cannot strip a taxpayer of substantial rights conferred by the contract. In Tangel, by contrast, the prohibition on reusing the research results was not an external statutory constraint—it was explicitly bargained for and written directly into Paragraph 15 of the private research agreement between Enercon and Vericor.
Procedural Consequence: Pretermitting Technical Substantiation

A critical second-order consequence of the ruling in Tangel is its demonstration of how the IRS utilizes summary judgment under Tax Court Rule 121 to bypass costly factual disputes over engineering qualification. Although the IRS also argued in its motion that petitioners had not substantiated the amount of QREs incurred on Project No. 37688, Judge Lauber held that because the four corners of the Vericor contract rendered the research 100% funded as a matter of law, the Court "need not address respondent's arguments about substantiation".

For tax practitioners, this establishes a rigid hierarchy of audit vulnerability in which contractual rights under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) operate as a threshold gatekeeper. Even if a taxpayer possesses comprehensive contemporaneous engineering documentation, prototype test logs, and W-2 wage tracking satisfying Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), a single "work made for hire" or unconditional non-use clause in the customer's standard purchase order terms can result in summary disallowance where, as in Tangel, the agreement as a whole leaves the contractor with no substantial rights without a single engineer ever testifying at trial.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory, regulatory, and evidentiary requirement addressed or implicated in Tangel v. Commissioner (and its companion Section 41 jurisprudence) against Enercon's specific legal or factual failure and the governing judicial standard of proof applied by the U.S. Tax Court.

Under Rule 121(b), a legal failure on funded research is dispositive on summary judgment, rendering factual proof of the Four-Part Test and QRE accounting moot.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the judicial holdings of Tangel v. Commissioner and subsequent federal appellate precedent into actionable tax and legal practice, the following two applied industry case studies examine realistic commercial engagements plagued by the exact contractual, governance, and evidentiary defects identified by Judge Lauber. For each scenario, a comprehensive, step-by-step remediation protocol is presented across contract drafting, project governance, technical documentation, and experimentation tracking.
Case Study 1: Custom Power Generation & Turbine Controls Integration (The Purchase Order "Battle of the Forms" Trap)
Industry Scenario and Initial Vulnerability Profile

AetherGrid Controls Corp. ("AetherGrid"), a U.S.-based S corporation specializing in custom medium-voltage switchgear, microgrid synchronization controllers, and acoustic turbine enclosures, is engaged by Apex Gas Turbines LLC ("Apex") to design and build an integrated control and enclosure package for a novel hydrogen-blended peaking turbine (Project H2-Peak). The commercial engagement is valued at $2.2 million across an initial purchase order and 12 subsequent engineering change orders.

At the outset of the engagement, AetherGrid's sales engineering team submits a technical quotation containing a cover letter stating that all custom enclosure drawings and control schematics developed for Project H2-Peak are proprietary to Apex. Apex subsequently issues its standard Purchase Order, which incorporates by reference Apex's standard "General Terms and Conditions of Procurement." Buried in Section 18 of Apex's terms is a "Designs, Tooling, and Data" clause virtually identical to Paragraph 15 in Tangel. Specifically, Section 18 defines "Buyer Data" as any technical information furnished by Apex or designed by AetherGrid at Apex's expense or to meet Apex's technical specifications. It prohibits AetherGrid from using "Buyer Data" or project tooling to manufacture or sell similar or interchangeable enclosures or controls to any third party without Apex's prior written consent. Furthermore, the purchase order provides for monthly progress billing based on timesheets and material invoices without formal technical acceptance milestones, while AetherGrid's engineers track their hours under a single blanket accounting job code ("Job #904 - Apex H2") without segregating routine assembly from experimental vibration and arc-flash modeling.

Under Tangel v. Commissioner and Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024), Project H2-Peak is 100% disqualified from Section 41 eligibility. AetherGrid retains no substantial rights under Section 18 of the contract, its cover letter constitutes an affirmative admission of "work for hire" divestiture, and its invoice-based payment schedule fails the financial risk test.
Step 1: Contractual Restructuring to Secure Substantial Rights

To neutralize the Tangel trap before purchase order execution, AetherGrid's legal and tax counsel must execute a "Master Engineering and Supply Addendum" that expressly supersedes conflicting boilerplate in Apex's General Terms and Conditions and eliminates the sales cover letter admission. First, the addendum must bifurcate client-specific deliverables from contractor background and foreground process intellectual property by redefining protected "Confidential Information" strictly as pre-existing technical specifications, turbine geometry, and operational data supplied by Apex to AetherGrid. This drafting modification excises the second and third prongs of the Tangel clause that fatally captured technical information designed by the contractor at the buyer's expense or to meet buyer-furnished specifications.

Second, the addendum must include an affirmative reservation of substantial rights and a non-exclusive commercial exploitation license. Specifically, the contract should state that notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the buyer's purchase order, AetherGrid retains all right, title, and interest in and to all engineering methodologies, thermodynamic and acoustic modeling techniques, control algorithms, switchgear architectures, and tooling designs developed or conceived during the performance of the agreement. To the extent title to specific physical deliverables or final assembly drawings vests in Apex, the addendum must grant AetherGrid an irrevocable, perpetual, worldwide, royalty-free, non-exclusive license—without any requirement of prior written consent or fee payment—to use, reproduce, modify, and commercially exploit all research results, engineering principles, and technical discoveries derived from the project in the design, manufacture, and sale of products for third-party customers, provided AetherGrid does not disclose Apex's pre-existing confidential information. This language directly satisfies Lockheed Martin, 210 F.3d at 1375, and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2)–(3) by guaranteeing an unconditional contractual right to use the research results without paying for that right or seeking unilateral client consent. Finally, counsel must strike any reverse burden-shifting provision requiring AetherGrid to prove non-use of Apex's funding or data when selling future switchgear or enclosures to third parties.
Step 2: Restructuring Payment Terms to Establish Financial Risk or Manage Partial Funding

Securing substantial rights prevents automatic 100% disqualification under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2), but AetherGrid must still satisfy or navigate the funding rules under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1) and (d)(3). To achieve full credit eligibility under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1) and Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995), AetherGrid must convert the contract from monthly progress invoicing to a fixed-price, performance-contingent agreement structured around verifiable technical acceptance milestones, such as Preliminary Acoustic and Thermal Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) Validation, Prototype Switchgear Arc-Flash Containment Testing, and Factory Acceptance Testing of the Integrated H2 Control Loop. The contract must explicitly stipulate that each milestone payment is contingent upon AetherGrid achieving objective, quantifiable technical performance barometers verified by formal inspection and evaluation. If the prototype fails to meet the specified technical thresholds and cannot be cured, Apex must hold the unconditional contractual right to reject the deliverables, terminate the contract for cause, and demand a full refund of any prior milestone advances, leaving AetherGrid bearing 100% of the financial cost of re-engineering, failed prototypes, and cost overruns.

Alternatively, if Apex insists on non-contingent time-and-materials progress payments on a specific change order (for example, Change Order #5 capped at $150,000), AetherGrid's retention of substantial rights in Step 1 preserves its eligibility for a partial credit allocation under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i)–(iii). Under this regulatory safe harbor, if AetherGrid incurs $240,000 of total research expenses to complete Change Order #5 while receiving only $150,000 in non-contingent funding, the $90,000 unfunded excess—or a pro rata allocation where total research expenses exceed funding and otherwise creditable expenses exceed 65 percent of the payment—remains fully eligible for the Section 41 credit on that project.
Step 3: Project Governance and Pre-Contract Gatekeeping

To prevent sales personnel from inadvertently waiving tax credits via informal offer letters—as occurred when Enercon wrote that all generated information and equipment were "owned by Vericor only -- 'works for hire'" in its summary letter—AetherGrid must institute a mandatory commercial-tax governance protocol. Sales engineers must be prohibited from drafting custom intellectual property ownership statements in bid letters; instead, all commercial quotations must incorporate a standardized "Reservation of Engineering Rights" clause stating that proposal pricing reflects AetherGrid's retention of non-exclusive rights to underlying engineering developments and tax attributes under IRC § 41. Additionally, any customer contract or purchase order exceeding $100,000 must pass a pre-execution legal and tax screening protocol designed to identify and strike the four Tangel red-flag phrases: "designed at Buyer's expense," "prior written consent," "works made for hire," and "exclusive right".
Step 4: Technical Documentation and Process of Experimentation Tracking

Once the contractual foundation is insulated from summary judgment under Rule 121, AetherGrid must construct its substantive evidentiary file to survive a trial on the merits under IRC § 41(d)(1) and Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023). Rather than defining the entire $2.2 million turbine package—which includes standard structural steel skids and commercial off-the-shelf circuit breakers—as a single business component, AetherGrid must apply the "shrinking-back rule" of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) to contemporaneously document discrete sub-component business components where genuine technological uncertainty exists, such as the Harmonic Damping Switchgear Busbar Assembly and the Negative-Pressure Hydrogen Leak Purge Control System.

For each discrete sub-component, engineers must maintain dated design review logs documenting the specific capability or design uncertainty, the formulation of competing engineering hypotheses, the systematic CFD and finite element analysis modeling runs and physical prototype iterations tested, and the empirical test data driving design modifications. Simultaneously, AetherGrid must replace its single blanket accounting job code ("Job #904") with phase-specific sub-codes that segregate experimental engineering design and prototype validation testing from routine commercial assembly and post-research commercial production excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(A). In strict compliance with Little Sandy Coal, supply costs (such as raw sheet metal and standard turbine components) must be tracked separately from employee research activities so that the 80% "substantially all" process-of-experimentation threshold under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) is substantiated strictly through employee activities rather than diluted by commercial material expenditures.
Case Study 2: Custom Industrial Automation & Embedded Control Software Engineering (The "Work Made for Hire" & Subcontractor Flow-Down Trap)
Industry Scenario and Initial Vulnerability Profile

VectraBotics Systems, Inc. ("VectraBotics"), a U.S. C corporation, designs custom robotic vision-guided welding cells and embedded real-time motion-control software for aerospace and defense prime contractors. VectraBotics enters into a Master Services Agreement (MSA) and Statement of Work (SOW #14) with Titan Aerospace Corp. ("Titan") for $1.8 million to develop a multi-axis laser-hybrid welding system capable of welding ultra-thin titanium-aluminide fuselage panels without thermal distortion. VectraBotics also hires an outside metallurgical testing firm, MetLab Inc., for $200,000 to perform specialized X-ray diffraction residual stress testing on experimental test welds.

The MSA drafted by Titan contains three critical provisions mirroring Paragraph 15(B) and 15(C) of Tangel as well as standard government-prime flow-down clauses. Section 12.1 of the MSA stipulates that all software source code, firmware, CAD models, test reports, and original works of authorship prepared by VectraBotics in connection with SOW #14 are "works made for hire" under U.S. Copyright Law owned exclusively by Titan, and to the extent any deliverable does not qualify as a work made for hire, VectraBotics "hereby irrevocably assigns all right, title, and interest, including all patent, copyright, and trade secret rights, to Titan". Section 12.2 mirrors Paragraph 15(C) of Tangel, requiring VectraBotics to insert the exact provisions of Section 12.1 into all subcontracts and purchase orders issued to third-party subcontractors, including MetLab Inc. Finally, Section 9 of the MSA provides that Titan will reimburse VectraBotics on a Cost-Plus-Fixed-Fee (CPFF) basis upon submission of bi-weekly labor and subcontractor expenditure vouchers.

Under Tangel v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-1, and Dynetics, Inc. v. United States, 121 Fed. Cl. 492 (2015), VectraBotics cannot claim a single dollar of in-house wages or the 65% contract research expense for MetLab Inc. Section 12.1 completely strips VectraBotics of substantial rights via the "work made for hire" and irrevocable assignment language, Section 12.2 transfers all rights in MetLab's research directly to Titan (meaning VectraBotics is not performing or procuring research on its own behalf under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)), and the CPFF reimbursement structure places zero financial risk on VectraBotics.
Step 1: Dismantling the "Work Made for Hire" and Blanket Assignment Trap

In custom software and automation engineering, clients legitimately demand ownership of the specific configuration files or physical machinery delivered to their factory floor, but they rarely require exclusive ownership of the underlying kinematics engines or reusable software libraries. To overcome Paragraph 15(B) of Tangel, VectraBotics must first strike the blanket "work made for hire" designation for software architecture, algorithms, and engineering data. Under U.S. copyright law (17 U.S.C. § 101), software and engineering designs created by an independent corporate contractor generally do not qualify as statutory "works made for hire" unless they fit within nine narrow statutory categories, making the fallback "irrevocable assignment" clause in Paragraph 15(B) a critical backstop (the Court did not decide whether Enercon's materials actually qualified as works made for hire, but noted that the text covers such Information even if a court determines it is not a work made for hire) in Tangel.

VectraBotics must redraft Section 12.1 of the MSA to architecturally decouple intellectual property across three explicit tiers. Tier 1 covers VectraBotics' pre-existing and core platform IP—including motion-control kernels, vision-processing libraries, and kinematics algorithms—which remain the sole property of VectraBotics. Tier 2 governs jointly exploitable research results and foreground innovations—encompassing all novel laser-pulse modulation algorithms, real-time thermal feedback control loops, and metallurgical process parameters discovered or developed during SOW #14—which shall either be owned by VectraBotics (with Titan receiving a non-exclusive license) or owned by Titan subject to an automatic, irrevocable, perpetual, non-exclusive, royalty-free commercial license back to VectraBotics to use, modify, and incorporate such research results into products and software sold to any third party without requiring Titan's prior written consent or paying any royalty. Tier 3 isolates Titan-specific part programs—solely the final G-code part trajectories and fixture CAD geometry specific to Titan's proprietary fuselage dimensions—which may be assigned exclusively to Titan without impairing VectraBotics' substantial rights in the underlying research.
Step 2: Reforming Subcontractor Flow-Down Clauses

In Tangel, Paragraph 15(C) required Enercon to flow down Vericor's restrictive IP terms to its subcontractors where such information was furnished to them for use in performing Vericor's orders. Under IRC § 41(b)(3) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(1)–(3), a taxpayer can claim 65% of contract research expenses paid to a third party (such as MetLab Inc.) only if the contract research is performed on behalf of the taxpayer prior to the performance of the research and the taxpayer retains substantial rights in the research results. Consequently, VectraBotics must modify Section 12.2 of the Titan MSA and its purchase order with MetLab Inc. so that MetLab performs the X-ray diffraction and residual stress research directly on behalf of VectraBotics, vesting the non-exclusive right to exploit MetLab's metallurgical test data and weld-parameter correlations in VectraBotics without restriction.
Step 3: Transforming CPFF Billing into At-Risk Fixed-Price Research Phases

Because a Cost-Plus-Fixed-Fee (CPFF) arrangement guarantees reimbursement of VectraBotics' costs regardless of technical outcome, it is treated as funded under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1), Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015), and Dynetics, Inc. v. United States, 121 Fed. Cl. 492 (2015). To remediate this defect, VectraBotics should split SOW #14 into two legally distinct contracts.

The first contract, SOW #14A, should cover Experimental Prototype and Control Algorithm Development as a $1.1 million fixed-price, at-risk agreement governed by strict contingency-of-success provisions satisfying Fairchild Industries and Meyer, Borgman & Johnson. Under SOW #14A, payment is earned only if the prototype robotic cell demonstrates weld porosity below 0.5% and thermal distortion under 0.15 mm across a 3-meter titanium-aluminide test coupon during formal Acceptance Testing. Until Titan executes the formal Certificate of Technical Acceptance, all progress draws are explicitly characterized as refundable advances that must be repaid in full if VectraBotics fails to achieve the contractual technical specifications. The second contract, SOW #14B, should isolate post-acceptance factory installation, operator training, and routine maintenance under a $700,000 time-and-materials arrangement. Because post-research commercial production and site installation are excluded from IRC § 41 under IRC § 41(d)(4)(A), segregating them into SOW #14B prevents time-and-materials billing terms from contaminating the fixed-price contingent risk profile of the qualified research under SOW #14A.
Step 4: Version-Controlled Experimentation Tracking and Audit Sampling Readiness

In Tangel—as well as subsequent Tax Court discovery disputes such as Kapur v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-28—disagreements over project sampling across large project populations created substantial procedural friction during litigation. To ensure full audit readiness across both technical experimentation and statistical sampling, VectraBotics must integrate its software engineering workflow directly with Section 41 tax substantiation. Every experimental software branch in Git and engineering epic in Jira under SOW #14A must be linked to a specific technical uncertainty record documenting the iterative process of experimentation: hypothesis formulation (such as evaluating a Kalman filter against a model predictive control loop for real-time laser power modulation), simulation results, physical laser weld coupon failures, and source code refactoring.

Furthermore, rather than waiting for an IRS audit or Tax Court petition to assemble a project list—which led to a Court-imposed sampling protocol in Tangel—VectraBotics must maintain an annual, contemporaneous Business Component Registry aligned with IRS statistical sampling standards. Each project entry in the registry must index the executed customer contract, a formal IP and Funding Legal Qualification Memorandum verifying substantial rights and payment contingency, W-2 employee timecards mapped to experimental tasks, third-party subcontractor agreements, and empirical test logs.
Summary Comparison of Remedial Restructuring Across Both Case Studies

Includes designs created by contractor at buyer's expense or to meet buyer's technical requirements (Paragraph 15(A)).

Express, irrevocable, perpetual, royalty-free, non-exclusive right to exploit all foreground research results without client consent or fee payment.

Architectural decoupling: contractor retains platform/process IP and foreground research rights; client receives title only to specific physical units or part programs.

Mandatory commercial-tax gatekeeping; standardized proposal rider reserving contractor's non-exclusive engineering rights and IRC § 41 tax attributes.

Subcontracts executed prior to research on behalf of the contractor, vesting substantial rights in the contractor under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e).
Payment & Financial Risk Structure
Non-contingent progress billing or Cost-Plus-Fixed-Fee (CPFF) invoicing.
Fixed-price, milestone-contingent contracts tied to objective technical acceptance testing with rejection/refund remedies (Fairchild standard).

body.text: 5. Strategic Conclusions and Practice Directives

The United States Tax Court's decision in Tangel v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-1, serves as an unmistakable warning to U.S. taxpayers and their tax advisors that technical innovation and engineering risk do not exist in a legal vacuum. Under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), the allocation of federal R&D tax credits between contracting parties is governed by the strict legal terms of their commercial agreements. When a custom manufacturer or engineering firm signs a customer purchase order containing sweeping "work made for hire" clauses, irrevocable IP assignments, or covenants prohibiting the reuse of project-developed designs without the customer's prior written consent, the taxpayer risks having the research on that project treated as fully funded and forfeiting 100% of the associated Section 41 research credits as a matter of law, as occurred with Project No. 37688 in Tangel.

To insulate R&D tax credit claims from summary disallowance under the Tangel doctrine, corporate tax departments and legal counsel must fundamentally realign their commercial contracting and tax substantiation workflows. Tax departments cannot wait until annual tax return preparation to review customer contracts; instead, legal and tax teams must integrate pre-execution contract riders into commercial procurement governance to automatically strike customer boilerplate restricting the reuse of contractor-developed designs, replacing those clauses with explicit reservations of non-exclusive commercial exploitation rights. Any contractual provision requiring a customer's prior written consent before the researcher can utilize engineering findings on future projects must either be eliminated or narrowed strictly to preventing the disclosure of the customer's pre-existing trade secrets.

Furthermore, practitioners conducting R&D tax credit studies must immediately disqualify—or flag for formal contractual remediation—any project where the taxpayer's sole claim to substantial rights rests on retaining general employee experience or construing a design-ownership clause as a routine non-disclosure agreement, as both arguments were rejected under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2) and Tangel. Finally, because post-Tangel jurisprudence—including Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024) and Smith v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-50 (2026)—rigorously enforces both prongs of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) even after Loper Bright, taxpayers must ensure that their commercial agreements pair the explicit retention of substantial rights with verifiable, success-contingent payment milestones.
